stories.topic: From Smuggled Chess Computers to Smuggled Nvidia Chips
stories.summary: Ajay remembers pre-1991 India, when protectionism made modern electronics almost impossible to buy. People relied on informal, black-market chains and on friends travelling abroad. His most prized purchase was an early chess computer whose LEDs blinked to show the next move, brought back by a neighbour flying to Singapore. Amit had the same one. You would expect this to be a distant memory. Instead, in Shanghai today you nudge, hint and wink to find the dealer with the right Nvidia A100. In Kazakhstan there is a bigger black market, where people fly in from New Delhi with suitcases of chips to sell at a profit.
stories.insight: Trade barriers don't make technology vanish. They push it underground. The world thought it was done with this kind of protectionism, yet the same back-channel economy has returned, this time created by export controls aimed at China.
stories.quote: And I find it amazing that in the streets of Shanghai, in the streets of Kazakhstan, you are now back to a black market for microchips.

stories.topic: When a Used Car Cost More Than a New One
stories.summary: For listeners born after 1991, Amit gives one fact that captures the old closed economy. A secondhand car cost more than a new one, because a new car had a seven-year waiting list while a used car was available immediately, whatever its condition. He points listeners to his Seen and the Unseen episode on the 1991 reforms with Ajay and Shruti Rajagopalan.
stories.insight: When shortages get bad enough, price stops reflecting quality and starts reflecting availability. Amit tells the story as a warning, since tariffs, industrial policy and protectionism are back and the world 'almost feels as if' it is going backwards.
stories.quote: a secondhand car costs more than a new car. Because a new car would have a wait list of seven years.

stories.topic: When India Was on the Wrong Side of Export Controls
stories.summary: In the late 1980s, the latest Sun SPARCstation workstations were not licensed for export to India, so you simply could not buy one here. Ajay calls them pitifully weak machines by modern standards. Until Manmohan Singh and George W. Bush signed the nuclear deal, US export controls on Indian buyers were extensive, and some remain even now.
stories.insight: Export controls are not a new weapon invented for China. India lived under them, and the Cold War blockade of the USSR is the template. What is new is the scale: the Bureau of Industry and Security, once fading in importance, has been revived into something bigger than it was even in the Cold War.
stories.quote: Now this is a pitifully weak CPU by modern standards. But export controls was a thing.

stories.topic: How NSE Built Its Risk System From Cheap CPUs
stories.summary: In the early 1990s, NSE wanted something never done before: derivatives risk management that ran in real time and covered every single participant, not just clearing members. Ashish Chauhan (now NSE's CEO) and Susan Thomas were sent to Chicago to pick between the CME's and CBOT's systems. Susan came back and told the leadership, Ravi Narayan and Chitra Ramakrishna, that both were dull 1970s technology. She proposed a Beowulf cluster instead: many cheap Intel CPUs computing in parallel. Each participant's risk could be calculated separately, so the work splits cleanly across CPUs. NSE's IT leadership thought the idea was crazy and that real time was impossible. Tempers flared, and Ravi Narayan split the difference by funding a proof of concept at IGIDR. The target was 100 calculations a second, beyond what the incumbents thought possible. Built with Shovam Mishra, the system, called PRISM, succeeded and, reworked over the years, still runs NSE's derivatives risk management today.
stories.insight: If a problem can be split into independent pieces, many cheap processors can match a few elite ones. Ajay uses this to argue that blocking top-end chips mostly makes a determined country's work slower and more painful, not impossible.
stories.quote: So this is an example that you can do so much by way of crazy high end computation, by stringing cheap CPUs in parallel.

recommendations.item: When the Chips Are Down
recommendations.creator: Pranay Kotasthane and Abhiram Manchi
recommendations.context: Amit's first pick in the recommendations segment. Pranay is a dear friend of both hosts.
recommendations.reason: Together with Chip War, it demystifies the semiconductor wars and what is really going on beneath the headlines.

recommendations.item: Chip War
recommendations.creator: Chris Miller
recommendations.context: Recommended alongside When the Chips Are Down in the closing segment.
recommendations.reason: It explains the semiconductor wars, the core battlefield of the US–China tech conflict discussed in the episode.

recommendations.item: How China Escaped the Poverty Trap
recommendations.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
recommendations.context: One of two books Amit recommends by a scholar he calls fantastic.
recommendations.reason: It is critical for understanding what has actually happened in China. It backs Amit's refusal to take a caricatured, good-versus-evil Cold War view of a deeply complex country, even while he largely agrees about the damage Xi Jinping is doing.

recommendations.item: China's Gilded Age
recommendations.creator: Yuen Yuen Ang
recommendations.context: Paired with How China Escaped the Poverty Trap in Amit's recommendations.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls both of Ang's books critical for understanding China's recent decades without falling into simplistic narratives.

recommendations.item: Michael Pettis interviewed by Forward Guidance
recommendations.creator: Forward Guidance (with Michael Pettis)
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation for the episode. It covers the Chinese macroeconomic story he deliberately set aside in the main discussion.
recommendations.reason: Pettis lives in China and, in Ajay's words, gets this stuff deeply. The interview is 'absolutely eye opening' on Chinese macroeconomics, the collapse of the China model, overproduction, and the global protectionism against China.

recommendations.item: The U.S. Finally Has a Strategy to Compete With China. Will It Work?
recommendations.creator: Greg Ip
recommendations.context: Amit opens the 'what is this great drama' chapter with this Wall Street Journal piece.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a wonderful piece that lays out the what and how of the shift, from a bipartisan pro-trade, engage-China consensus to a new bipartisan consensus that America is at war with China.

recommendations.item: 'An Act of War': Inside America's Silicon Blockade Against China
recommendations.creator: Alex W Palmer
recommendations.context: A New York Times piece Amit calls great. He reads from it to explain the FDPR.
recommendations.reason: It shows how far the US now reaches: goods made and shipped entirely outside America, with no US components, can still count as American goods if American technology or software was used to make them.

recommendations.item: Three holes in the U.S.' economic strategy against China
recommendations.creator: Noah Smith
recommendations.context: Amit cites Noah Smith's newsletter discussion of China's drone dominance.
recommendations.reason: It makes the point Amit wants: instead of export restrictions, America could deregulate its own industry so more people build drones at home. This is his model for answering cheap Chinese imports through domestic freedom rather than bans.

recommendations.item: The tech wars are about to enter a fiery new phase
recommendations.creator: The Economist
recommendations.context: Linked right after Amit's quip about the BIS.
recommendations.reason: It argues, correctly in Amit's view, that these tech and trade wars are bad for the US, bad for China and bad for the rest of the world.

recommendations.item: Knowledge Lost and Knowledge Regained (Episode 63 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit opens by noting that the world hasn't learned the lessons of the previous episode. Ajay links back to its thought experiment about rebuilding a pencil from scratch.
recommendations.reason: It explains why being cut off from global trade and knowledge cripples a country: it is very hard to make a pencil, let alone an iPhone, on your own.

recommendations.item: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recommended to listeners born after 1991 who can't picture how bad India's closed economy was.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great episode that brings alive the bizarre pre-1991 world the episode warns we might be drifting back toward.

recommendations.item: The Reformers (Episode 28 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Part of the 'bunch of episodes' on the 1991 reforms that Amit urges listeners to check out.
recommendations.reason: It gives background on how India escaped the protectionist era the hosts describe.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes with the set of episodes Amit asks listeners to check out after describing the pre-1991 era.
recommendations.reason: It is companion listening on why the closed, unfree economy failed.

recommendations.item: The Three Globalizations (Episode 17 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay says the tech wars are deeply related to this episode and are an intensification of the third globalization.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the framework behind today's discussion: access to the advanced-economy core is now conditional on good behaviour in military and foreign affairs.

recommendations.item: Dawn of the third globalisation?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit mentions Ajay's column while steel-manning, and then disagreeing with, the third-globalization idea.
recommendations.reason: It is the written version of Ajay's 'novel insight' that globalization hasn't ended but now excludes rogue players.

recommendations.item: The China Model is Broken (Episode 16 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay refers to it while explaining how Xi Jinping's rule broke China's economic model.
recommendations.reason: It is background on Xi's centralisation, the exit of foreigners and capitalists, and the macro meltdown. Ajay says they were on the right track there.

recommendations.item: The case for trade barriers against Chinese imports
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit links it while voicing his disagreement with Ajay over restrictions on Chinese goods.
recommendations.reason: It is the other side of the hosts' disagreement. Read it next to Amit's argument that even unilateral free trade benefits people on both sides.

recommendations.item: The BIS list of sanctions
recommendations.creator: Bureau of Industry and Security
recommendations.context: Ajay calls this 'knowledge that you can use' and urges listeners to hang out on the BIS website.
recommendations.reason: Anyone in business should know who is on the list. Dealing with a listed entity can land you in trouble, and being listed (about 12 Indian entities are) cuts you off from US travel, finance and trade.

recommendations.item: The Outlaws (Episode 61 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay references 'our beautiful EIE episode on Outlaws' while explaining why the USSR couldn't catch up.
recommendations.reason: The geniuses who drive breakthroughs are mavericks and 'crazy people', exactly the people authoritarian societies crush.

recommendations.item: The Semiconductor Wars (Episode 358 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Abhiram Manchi
recommendations.context: Amit mentions his 'great episode' with the authors of When the Chips Are Down while discussing China's legacy-chip push and India's chip ambitions.
recommendations.reason: It is a long-form deep dive on chips to accompany the book recommendations.

core_ideas.explanation: Until about 2016, Democrats and Republicans agreed that free trade was good and that America should engage with China. It felt like an 'end of history' moment. Doubts began inside the Obama administration, including from Jake Sullivan. Trump then won partly through simple, wrong but easy-to-grasp narratives: immigrants and trade are taking your jobs. Biden promised to reverse Trump's policies, but his own team split. Janet Yellen wanted lower tariffs; Katherine Tai wanted higher ones. Biden sided with Sullivan's hawkish view. In eight years the consensus flipped to the opposite pole.
core_ideas.quote: You know, in just eight years, everything is switched around, and the consensus now is that we are at war with China.

core_ideas.concept: The Three-Legged Stool of the Tech War
core_ideas.explanation: America's campaign rests on three legs. Industrial policy: heavy subsidies, such as those that drew TSMC to build fabs in Arizona (Amit notes India tried industrial policy in the 1950s–60s). Tariffs: rising under both Trump and Biden. Export controls: cutting off the IP, chips and tools China needs to develop indigenously. Chips matter so much because modern science runs on large-scale simulation, which needs high-powered compute.
core_ideas.quote: So this is the three prong stool, you know? Industrial policy, tariffs and export control.

core_ideas.concept: Extraterritorial Export Controls and the FDPR
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says the only comparable precedent is the pre-1989 Western blockade of the USSR, and now Japan, the Netherlands and Germany have joined in. ASML's most advanced machines can't go to China or Russia. Neither can the three American software systems all chip design depends on. An Indian firm using American tools to design chips for a Chinese customer gets sanctioned too. US citizens and green-card holders can't work in these Chinese sectors. The Foreign Direct Product Rule goes furthest: goods made abroad with American technology or software count as American even if they never touch US soil. Huawei was its first major target.
core_ideas.quote: if any company anywhere in the world will use American tools, American software, and do work for a Chinese customer, then they will be sanctioned as well.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that US engagement with China was not just interests and realpolitik but genuine idealism, something Indians struggle to picture. He says he has seen it face to face. After Nixon's 1972 opening and Deng's rise in 1978, American society and the state signed on to 'the China project'. After 1989, the end-of-history mood held that China would wise up into a free-market liberal democracy if given time. So the West handed over technology, investment and trade, and Bill Clinton championed China's entry into the WTO.
core_ideas.quote: all through the twentieth century there has been a sense in America that China is our responsibility

core_ideas.concept: Why the West Turned: Misbehaviour Times Size
core_ideas.explanation: China largely failed to keep its WTO promises. On top of that came state-backed IP theft and cyber attacks. India has also misbehaved on trade, keeping protectionism while demanding openness, but India was small enough not to matter. China became systemically important. Then Russia invaded Ukraine, arguably funded by European gas purchases and fought with weapons built on German machine tools and Western electronics. Xi Jinping doubled down: he backed Russia, rattled sabres over Taiwan, and acted as a 'revisionist power' that seeks to overturn the international order by force. The West concluded it was arming its own adversaries.
core_ideas.quote: India is inconsequential, so you know a little bit of misbehavior here and there in terms of protectionism in India doesn't materially move the needle. In contrast, China became big.

core_ideas.concept: The Third Globalization: Conditional Access to the Core
core_ideas.explanation: In the second globalization, the advanced-economy core (about 65% of world GDP) gave the periphery unconditional access to capital, technology and markets. The only barriers were the periphery's own, such as India's. In the third globalization, access depends on good behaviour in military and foreign affairs. Ajay presents this first as a description of how the world now works, separate from the question of whether it is wise.
core_ideas.quote: Access to globalization is no longer a free lunch

core_ideas.concept: Economic Warfare Beats Real Warfare (Ajay's Position)
core_ideas.explanation: As an economist, Ajay wants world peace and full globalization. But if the trade-off is between killing people and limiting a rogue power's prosperity, he chooses the second. The old saying that two countries with McDonald's never go to war no longer holds. With a hot war under way and Xi refusing to renounce invading Taiwan, he sees the tech war as a reasonable strategy.
core_ideas.quote: It is better to do economic warfare than to do real warfare.

core_ideas.concept: Economic Warfare Is Economic Warfare (Amit's Position)
core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues that freedom and voluntary exchange should be foundational, not contingent. A selective globalization is no more globalization than crony capitalism is capitalism. Who defines the 'global order' America claims to enforce? Trade is positive-sum, so the Swiss keeping zero tariffs on India is not a favour but in their own interest. Economic warfare hurts ordinary people on both sides while states play games. The answer to cheap Chinese imports or drone dominance is to deregulate your own industry. If local doctors are poor, train them up through competition rather than banning foreign doctors, or the patient dies. He admits he has no answer to IP theft or the Taiwan threat.
core_ideas.quote: But to me economic warfare is economic warfare, and I'm fundamentally against economic warfare at all times.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says Deng failed because his project of making China a normal country collapsed under Xi. By that standard, he says, he would even call the US Constitution wrong if Trump cancelled democracy. Amit strongly disagrees. Deng lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty and raised the odds of a better political outcome. Blaming him for Xi is like saying Nehru failed had Indira Gandhi not called off the Emergency. The debate is about whether to judge leaders by long-run end states or by the probabilities they improved.
core_ideas.quote: Hundreds of millions of people out of poverty means hundreds and millions of successes.

core_ideas.concept: Why Self-Reliance Under Sanctions Fails in Authoritarian States
core_ideas.explanation: Western export controls helped win the Cold War. Cut off from Western tech, the USSR tried self-reliance and never caught up: it never built competitive computers or got to Unix. Part of the reason is that recreating a vast body of knowledge and artifacts is enormously hard. The other part is that authoritarian regimes crush the tiny fraction of maverick geniuses who would have done the catching up.
core_ideas.quote: The best minds don't flourish when they are crushed under conditions of unfreedom.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay notes that a determined person can do a lot without state-of-the-art equipment. Modern parallel computing strings together many weaker processors, and that capability exists in India, China and Russia. So chip bans mostly add delay and pain. For a defence lab simulating a nuclear explosion, they are not material.
core_ideas.quote: Instead of 10 super duper powerful modern Nvidia GPUs, you'll have 1000 weaker GPUs, you will get to the same compute.

core_ideas.concept: Sanctions Work on Races, Not Fixed Targets
core_ideas.explanation: Against a fixed goal like a nuclear bomb, export controls are useless: the sanctioned country gets there eventually. In a race, only relative position matters. Examples are the drone war over Ukraine, artillery quality, or winner-takes-all product markets. A one- or two-month lag in DJI's or Russia's drone design could let Ukrainian drones win on the battlefield, and small technology edges can shift global market share. Ajay stresses that the jury is still out on whether this will work against China.
core_ideas.quote: You don't need to indefinitely be better. You only need to be a little bit better.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit warns that the logic sounds great but the real world reacts. Squeezing China could make it more desperate over Taiwan. China is already ramping up legacy chips and could wipe out that business for TSMC, Intel and Samsung, which would also sink India's chip ambitions. He compares this to America's arrogance in arming Afghan guerrillas, including Osama bin Laden. Ajay agrees there will be surprises and adds a nuance: a drone needs mostly simple legacy chips plus one or a few high-end CPUs, so China may come to dominate legacy chips globally.
core_ideas.quote: all of this rationale sounds great, but unintended consequences will compound.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay separates three overlapping stories. The third globalization: access to the core becoming conditional, with the Trump tariffs of 2016–18 as one big trigger. The tech war: a military-driven escalation from 2022, with the sweeping US export restrictions of 7 October 2022 as the key milestone. And a short-term Chinese macroeconomic problem of overproduction from the last year or two. Mixing them up muddles the debate.
core_ideas.quote: So there are three distinct stories going on.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the export-control agency: 'At the risk of being sanctioned by the US BIS, I will say that the US BIS should be renamed US BS.'

Amit: 'as Donald Trump would say, in all caps, we have the best plans. But the great geopolitical and military strategist Mike Tyson once said that the best plan only survives till you get punched in the face.' Ajay corrects the soundbite to 'everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth', and Amit counter-corrects: 'It's not everybody, it's everyone.'

Ajay explains parallel computing by noting that the calculation for Amit is independent of the one for producer Nomsita. Amit: 'neither me nor Nomsita understood exactly that parallel whatever you were saying. But you spoke about multiplying our power, so I'm kinda happy with that.'

Ajay on India negotiating a free trade agreement with Switzerland: 'the humor of this is the Swiss have no tariffs against anything from India. So what are you going to negotiate? The Swiss say we are already at zero.'
Francis Fukuyama's 'end of history', which Amit calls an 'often misinterpreted phrase'. It was the 1990s mood in which the West assumed liberal democracy and free markets were the only game in town.
Ajay's sketch of the post-1989 euphoria: 'This entire nightmare of 2000 years of fighting between Persia and Athens has come to an end, and Athens won.'
The old saying that two countries with McDonald's never go to war. Ajay: 'Well, Russia invaded Ukraine and both countries had McDonald's.'
'Where you stand depends on where you sit': Amit's aside on why Biden's trade chief Katherine Tai pushed for higher tariffs while Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen wanted engagement.
Amit cites America's Cold War move in Afghanistan, funding guerrillas including Osama bin Laden against the Soviets, as the classic case of unintended consequences from trying to shape the world.

The Bureau of Industry and Security, which Ajay calls an obscure agency and 'one of the most consequential government organizations in the whole world'. Amit adds that it issued about 100,000 export licences a year at its Cold War peak, around 10,000 in the 1990s, and is back to about 40,000.

The pencil thought experiment from the previous episode: if all artifacts vanished, 'we're just a bunch of seven and a half billion naked people wandering the world. How will we ever build a pencil again?' Ajay uses it to show why a country cut off from global knowledge struggles to catch up.
